food.text: Around 9700 BCE, climate warming increased wild food resources in China and reduced nomadism. Hunter-gatherers moved less and began to store supplies, often stocks of acorns. This set the stage for the shift to farming.

The Neolithic in China was an economic revolution in which people learned to produce their own food by domesticating plants and animals. Neolithization mainly occurred between 7000 and 5000 BCE. Pottery had appeared much earlier, among Late Paleolithic populations, so it was a separate development.

Millet and rice were first gathered and eaten in their wild forms, then gradually domesticated around 6000 to 5000 BCE. Wild rice was domesticated in the Lower Yangtze region, while millet was domesticated in the Yellow River basin in Henan. At first they contributed only a little to the diet, competing with other wild plants and hunted foods.
From around 5000 BCE, agriculture became a much more significant part of the Chinese diet. Underground silos were often used to store certain plant-based foods.

The Peiligang and Cishan cultures (Cishan dated 6500 to 5000 BCE) are regarded as the first established agricultural peoples in China. Their remains suggest settled life and the use of millet as the main crop. Their pottery was mostly simple bowls and jars.

Rice farming in southern China was once thought to have begun around 5000 BCE, but newer research has pushed the start back to as early as 7500 BCE. At Diaotonghuan in Jiangxi, evidence suggests that even around 10000 BCE people were already shifting from gathering wild rice to farming it.

Irrigated rice fields appeared in Zhejiang around 4000 BCE. At the Kuahuqiao site (6000 to 5500 BCE), archaeologists found irrigation canals and wells. Early rice farming in the region had generally relied on drainage methods before irrigation became common.

Jiahu, a prominent Peiligang site covering 5.5 hectares, belonged to a millet-farming culture. Yet excavations there have also yielded examples of rice. This suggests the people used an alternative food strategy alongside millet.

Southern China was known for early pottery-making, which appeared around the 12th millennium BCE. In China, agriculture seems to have begun at the same time as pottery production and sedentary life, unlike in many other regions.

At Tianluoshan (5000 to 3000 BCE), rice was cultivated and was in the process of being domesticated. Even so, the people of the Hemudu culture largely relied on the abundant natural resources around them for food.
The Houli culture in Shandong (c. 6200 to 5500 BCE) shared similar characteristics with Peiligang and Cishan. However, traces of millet agriculture have yet to be found there.

art.text: Chinese art is said to reach back to about 10,000 BC with what is called Stone Age art. It mostly consisted of simple pottery and sculptures. After that period, Chinese art was usually sorted by the succession of ruling dynasties.

The Yangshao culture, dating back to the 6th millennium BC, made pottery at sites such as Banpo. Early ceramics were unpainted and most often cord-marked. The first decorations were fish, human faces, and plants, images familiar from their farming lifestyles.

The oldest known lacquered object in the world, a wooden bowl, was discovered at the Hemudu site. Hemudu also produced body ornaments in fluorite and "pseudo-jade" as early as its Period I, followed later by developed jade craftsmanship.

Jade production began in China over seven millennia ago, around 5000 BCE. It yielded the largest body of intricately crafted jade artifacts created by any single civilization. Native sources in Henan and along the Yangtze were used since prehistoric times.

Stilted lake dwellings discovered at Hemudu in 1973 came as a major surprise. They contrasted sharply with the earthen dwellings of northern China, which had seemed to be the origin and center of Chinese culture. The stilt houses often show expertise in mortise-and-tenon joint construction.

Seven thousand years ago, mortise and tenon joinery was used to build wood-framed houses, and the oldest are at the Hemudu site in Zhejiang. During the Middle Neolithic Yangshao culture, circular and rectangular semisubterranean structures had wooden beams and columns. Their roofs were most likely thatched.

Yangshao pottery decoration grew more colorful, intricate, and abstract over time, with geometric and astronomy-inspired patterns. Unlike the later Longshan culture, the Yangshao did not use pottery wheels and relied on manual techniques like coiling. Late-phase pieces with parallel lines and grids suggest that a spinning method was used to paint the pottery.

Hemudu pottery was often black, with uneven wall thickness, and during Period I firing temperatures barely exceeded 800 degrees Celsius. By the final period, ceramics were fired at relatively high temperatures, were thin and sturdy, and were shaped using a slow-turning wheel and at times a fast wheel.

A typical pottery ding from the fourth millennium BCE had flat legs positioned radially, with leg edges either pinched or serrated. These tripods traced their origins back to early Neolithic versions made by the Peiligang and Yangshao. The early bronze ding was probably inspired by this design.

Symmetry mattered in early Chinese building. As Neolithic villages and towns grew, they adhered to symmetrical shapes, and symmetry was also important in the layout of homes, altars, and villages. Yet it is not known how the builders got the huge wooden support columns into position.

war.text: The Xinglongwa culture, which existed from 6200 to 5400 BC in the Liao River basin of northeastern China, built the earliest site in China known to have been surrounded by a ditch. This ditch enclosed the settlement at its type site in Aohan Banner, Inner Mongolia, an early form of fortification.

During the Late Yangshao period, around 3500 to 3000 BC, the settlement of Xishan in central Henan near modern Zhengzhou was enclosed by the first wall of rammed earth ever built in China. The wall enclosed an area of about 25 hectares, marking a new stage of fortified settlement building in the region.

At Xinglongwa's type site in Aohan Banner, Chifeng, 120 pit-houses stood protected within the settlement's surrounding ditch, each home built around a central hearth. This communal layout, with a large central building, shows organized planning behind China's earliest known ditch fortification.

Earlier in the Yangshao culture, the settlements of Banpo and Jiangzhai in the Wei River valley of Shaanxi were enclosed by ring-ditches. When archaeologists excavated Jiangzhai to its limits, they found it was completely surrounded by one such ditch.

science.text: Southern China was among the earliest places to make pottery, which appeared around the 12th millennium BCE. In China, agriculture seems to have begun at the same time as pottery production and sedentary life, unlike in many other regions.

Around 9700 BCE, climate warming increased wild food resources and reduced nomadism in China. Hunter-gatherers moved less and began to store supplies, often stocks of acorns, which paved the way for the Neolithic economic revolution.

Wild rice was gradually domesticated in the Lower Yangtze region around 6000 to 5000 BCE, while millet was domesticated in the Yellow River basin in Henan. At first both made only a minor contribution to the diet, but from around 5000 BCE agriculture became far more important.

At Diaotonghuan in Jiangxi, evidence suggests that by 10000 BCE people were already moving from gathering wild rice to farming it. Later research pushed the start of rice cultivation in southern China back to as early as 7500 BCE.

At the Kuahuqiao site in Zhejiang, dated to 6000 to 5500 BCE, archaeologists found irrigation canals and wells. Early rice farming there used drainage methods, and irrigated fields followed in Zhejiang around 4000 BCE.

The stilted lake dwellings of the Hemudu culture, discovered in 1973, were a major surprise because they contrasted so sharply with the earthen dwellings of northern China. The stilt houses often show expertise in mortise-and-tenon joint construction.

The oldest known lacquered object in the world, a wooden bowl, was discovered at the Hemudu site. It is an early sign of the craft skill of the people living in the warm, humid region south of Hangzhou Bay.

Hemudu potters improved their technology over time. In Period I, firing temperatures barely exceeded 800 °C, but in the final period ceramics were fired at relatively high temperatures, made thin and sturdy, and shaped using a slow-turning wheel, and at times a fast wheel.

The Jiahu Gudi, unearthed at the Jiahu site and dated between 7,000 and 5,700 years ago, is the earliest, best-preserved and most numerous musical instrument in the world that can still be played. A tortoiseshell there also bears 16 Jiahu symbols from about 6600 BCE, though they cannot be conclusively identified as writing.

politics.text: During the Late Yangshao period, about 3500 to 3000 BCE, settlement hierarchies spread across the middle Yellow River valley. The first rammed-earth wall in China was built around this time, enclosing the 25-hectare settlement of Xishan in central Henan, near modern Zhengzhou.

In the Dawenkou culture of eastern China, grave goods from the early phase, about 4100 to 3500 BCE, show a highly egalitarian society. By the middle phase, roughly 3500 to 3000 BCE, grave goods began to emphasize quantity over diversity, an early sign of growing social ranking.

The Liangzhu culture, which began around 3300 BCE in the Yangtze River Delta, is considered one of China's earliest state societies. Jade, silk, ivory and lacquer artifacts were found exclusively in elite burials, while poorer individuals were buried mainly with pottery.

Earlier, during the Middle Yangshao period's Miaodigou phase, about 4000 to 3500 BCE, the culture's population and territory expanded in all directions. Settlement hierarchies also began to develop in some areas, such as western Henan, ahead of the walled centers built later.

During Dawenkou's early phase, individually designed long-stemmed cups were common grave goods. Graves built with earthen ledges also became increasingly common toward the end of this period, just ahead of the culture's later shift toward greater social stratification.

Liangzhu City, founded around 3300 BCE in Hangzhou, included a walled centre with palatial complexes, ceremonial areas and an intricate hydraulic system. This hydraulic system is by far the earliest known one in the world, and points to a highly centralised system of governance.

At the Yaoshan site near Liangzhu City, dated to around 3300 to 3100 BC, archaeologists found 678 jade artefacts at an altar and a noble tomb, including jade yue axes alongside jade cong. These pieces symbolised power and belief, predating the construction of the city.

A pan-regional urban centre emerged at the Liangzhu site in northwestern Hangzhou, with elite groups based there presiding over smaller local centres. Liangzhu's sphere of influence reached as far north as Shanxi and as far south as Guangdong.

At the Yaoshan site, an early part of Liangzhu City dating to about 3300 to 3100 BCE, an altar and a noble tomb predating the city yielded 678 jade artefacts, including jade cong and jade yue that symbolised power. Archaeologists see this as evidence of social stratification before the city itself was built.

The Majiayao culture of the upper Yellow River, which began around 3300 BCE, produced painted pottery at large centralised workshops, including the largest Neolithic workshop found in China, at Baidaogouping in Gansu. This scale of production required professional craftspeople, taken as evidence of increasing social complexity.

Across Neolithic China, starting around 5000 BC, jade workers crafted ritual versions of ordinary tools and weapons. These jade pieces were often larger than the originals and too impractical for real use, and are thought to have been symbols of political power or religious authority rather than actual combat gear.

Among the jade artefacts found at Yaoshan, dated to around 3300 to 3100 BCE, was a 6.5-kilogram carved cong known as the 'King of Cong.' It was one of the objects buried with Liangzhu's elite as a symbol of power and status.

culture.text: The Hemudu people lived in long stilt houses, and communal longhouses were also common at their sites. The site, discovered in 1973, belonged to a people who are said to have differed physically from the inhabitants of the Yellow River sites to the north.

Hemudu's inhabitants worshiped a sun spirit as well as a fertility spirit, and enacted shamanistic rituals to the Sun and believed in bird totems. A belief in an afterlife and ghosts is thought to have been widespread. The dead were buried with their heads facing east or northeast, most with no burial objects, and infants were buried in urn-casket style burials while children and adults received earth level burials.

Excavators at Niuheliang found an underground temple complex with an altar, stone platforms and painted walls. Archaeologists named it the "Goddess Temple" after a clay female head with jade inlaid eyes was discovered there.

The Dawenkou practiced dental ablation and cranial deformation, and many of their burials show both. Between 60 and 90 percent of people had teeth removed, with no difference between the sexes. The upper incisors and canines were pulled most often, then the lower incisors, and most teeth appear to have been knocked out between the ages of 13 and 15. Both customs had disappeared from mainland China by the start of the Bronze Age.
A red lacquer wood bowl held at the Zhejiang Museum is dated to 4000-5000 BC. It is believed to be the earliest such object in the world, and it came from the Hemudu culture.
Inside the Goddess Temple stood clay figurines as large as three times the size of real-life humans. They are possibly deities, though for a religion not reflected in any other Chinese culture.

Archaeologist Su Bingqi argued from Hongshan and Yangshao ritual constructions that a religious transition occurred during the fourth millennium BCE. He believed it produced a group of religious professionals by 3500 BCE.

The Peiligang people fished for carp in the nearby river using nets made from hemp fibers, and they hunted deer and wild boar. They also raised pigs and cultivated millet, and their villages typically had separate residential and burial areas.

A skull of a Dawenkou man dating to 3000 BC was found with severe head injuries that appeared to have been remedied by trepanation. Dawenkou's inhabitants were among the earliest practitioners of this primitive surgery in prehistoric China.
Guo Dashun believes that the Hongshan culture had a mature system of ancestral worship. He holds that this practice remained important throughout all of Chinese history.

The Hongshan culture of northeast China, dated from about 4700 to 2900 BC, is known for its carved jade. Its burial artifacts include some of the earliest known examples of jade working, such as jade pig dragons. Clay figurines, including figurines of pregnant women, are also found throughout Hongshan sites.
